arXiv:1610.05387v2 [math.CO] 01 Mar 2017

Conjectures involving a generalization of the sums of powers of integers

Andrei K. Svinin Address: Andrei K. Svinin, Matrosov Institute for System Dynamics and Control Theory of Siberian Branch of Russian Academy of Sciences, P.O. Box 292, 664033 Irkutsk, Russia Email address: svinin@icc.ru
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

Some class of sums which naturally include the sums of powers of integers is considered. A number of conjectures concerning a representation of these sums is made.

1. Introduction

It is common knowledge that the sum of powers of integers

Sm​(n):=∑q=1nqmS_{m}(n):=\sum_{q=1}^{n}q^{m} (1.1)

is a polynomial σm​(n)\sigma_{m}(n) in nn of degree m+1m+1. This proposition can be showed by using Pascal’s elementary proof (see, for example [1]). Polynomials σm​(n)\sigma_{m}(n) for any integer m≥1m\geq 1 are defined in terms of the Bernoulli numbers:

σm​(n)=1m+1​∑q=0m(−1)q​(m+1q)​Bq​nm−q+1.\sigma_{m}(n)=\frac{1}{m+1}\sum_{q=0}^{m}(-1)^{q}{m+1\choose q}B_{q}n^{m-q+1}.

The numbers BkB_{k}, in turn, are defined by a recursion

∑q=0k(k+1q)​Bq=0,B0=1.\sum_{q=0}^{k}{k+1\choose q}B_{q}=0,\;\;B_{0}=1.

They were discovered by Bernoulli in 1713 but as explained in [4], they were known by Faulhaber before this time.

Faulhaber’s theorem says that for any odd m≥3m\geq 3, the sum (1.1) is expressed as a polynomial of S1​(n)S_{1}(n). It is common knowledge that S1​(n)=n⁡(n+1)/2S_{1}(n)=n(n+1)/2. Let us denote t:=n⁡(n+1)t:=n(n+1). Therefore, the Faulhaber’s theorem asserts that for any k≥1k\geq 1, S2​k+1​(n)S_{2k+1}(n) can be expressed as a polynomial in ℚ⁡[t]\mathbb{Q}[t]. These polynomials are referred as Faulhaber’s polynomials. Also, it is worth remembering that it was shown by Jacobi in [10] that S2​k​(n)S_{2k}(n) is expressed as a polynomial in (2​n+1)​ℚ​[t](2n+1)\mathbb{Q}[t].

There exists a variety of different modifications and generalizations of Faulhaber’s theorem in the literature. Faulhaber himself considered rr-fold sums Smr​(n)S_{m}^{r}(n) which are successively defined by

Smr​(n)=∑q=1nSmr−1​(q),r≥1S_{m}^{r}(n)=\sum_{q=1}^{n}S_{m}^{r-1}(q),\;\;r\geq 1

beginning from Sm0​(n):=nmS_{m}^{0}(n):=n^{m}. He observed that Smr​(n)S_{m}^{r}(n) can be expressed as a polynomial in n⁡(n+r)n(n+r) if m−rm-r is even [11].

In this paper we consider some class of sums Sk,j​(n)S_{k,j}(n) which include classical sums of powers of integers (1.1) with odd m=2​k+1m=2k+1. These sums will be introduced in section 2 and 3. In the particular case n=1n=1, they represent some class of binomial sums studied in [15]. Our crucial idea comes from this work. We briefly describe the results of this article in section 4. In section 5, we formulate our main conjecture concerning a representation of the sums Sk,j​(n)S_{k,j}(n) in terms of some polynomials whose coefficients rationally depend on nn. In section 6, we discuss the relationship of this representation with a possible generalization of the Faulhaber’s theorem. In section 7, we show the explicit form of some nn-dependent coefficients of these polynomials and speculate about the relationship of these coefficients with the number of qq-points in the simple symmetric (2​k+1)(2k+1)-Venn diagram.

2. The sums sk,j​(n)s_{k,j}(n)

Let us define the numbers {Cj,r(n):j≥1,r=0,…,j(n−1)}\{C_{j,r}(n):j\geq 1,r=0,\ldots,j(n-1)\} through the relation

(∑q=0n−1aq+1)j=∑q=0j⁡(n−1)Cj,q​(n)​aq+j,\left(\sum_{q=0}^{n-1}a^{q+1}\right)^{j}=\sum_{q=0}^{j(n-1)}C_{j,q}(n)a^{q+j}, (2.1)

where aa is supposed to be an auxiliary variable, taking into account that al​am=al+ma^{l}a^{m}=a^{l+m}. For example, in the case n=1n=1, we have only Cj,0​(1)=1C_{j,0}(1)=1, while in the case n=2n=2, we get

(a+a2)j=∑q=0j(jq)​aj+q,\left(a+a^{2}\right)^{j}=\sum_{q=0}^{j}{j\choose q}a^{j+q},

and therefore Cj,q​(2)C_{j,q}(2) is a binomial coefficient. From

(∑q=0n−1aq+1)j\displaystyle\left(\sum_{q=0}^{n-1}a^{q+1}\right)^{j} =\displaystyle= (∑q=0(j−1)​(n−1)Cj−1,q​(n)​aq+j−1)​(∑q=0n−1aq+1)\displaystyle\left(\sum_{q=0}^{(j-1)(n-1)}C_{j-1,q}(n)a^{q+j-1}\right)\left(\sum_{q=0}^{n-1}a^{q+1}\right)
=\displaystyle= Cj−1,0​(n)​aj+(Cj−1,0​(n)+Cj−1,1​(n))​aj+1+⋯+(Cj−1,0​(n)+⋯CLOSE\displaystyle C_{j-1,0}(n)a^{j}+\left(C_{j-1,0}(n)+C_{j-1,1}(n)\right)a^{j+1}+\cdots+\left(C_{j-1,0}(n)+\cdots\right.
OPEN+Cj−1,n−1​(n))​aj+n−1\displaystyle\left.+C_{j-1,n-1}(n)\right)a^{j+n-1}
+(Cj−1,1​(n)+⋯+COPENj−1,n)​(n))​aj+n+⋯+Cj−1,(j−1)​(n−1)​(n)​aj​n\displaystyle+\left(C_{j-1,1}(n)+\cdots+C_{j-1,n)}(n)\right)a^{j+n}+\cdots+C_{j-1,(j-1)(n-1)}(n)a^{jn}

we deduce that

Cj,r​(n)=∑q=r−n+1rCj−1,q​(n)C_{j,r}(n)=\sum_{q=r-n+1}^{r}C_{j-1,q}(n) (2.2)

in assumption that Cj−1,q​(n)=0C_{j-1,q}(n)=0 for q<0q<0 and q>(j−1)​(n−1)q>(j-1)(n-1). In the case n=2n=2, the relation (2.2) becomes a well-known property for the binomial coefficients:

(jr)=(j−1r−1)+(j−1r).{j\choose r}={j-1\choose r-1}+{j-1\choose r}.

Clearly, the coefficient Cj,r​(n)C_{j,r}(n) can be represented as a proper sum of multinomial coefficients. Putting a=1a=1 into (2.1), we get the property

∑q=0j⁡(n−1)Cj,q​(n)=nj\sum_{q=0}^{j(n-1)}C_{j,q}(n)=n^{j}

for these numbers which evidently generalize the well-known attribute of binomial coefficients. Also it is easy to get the following property:

∑q=0j⁡(n−1)q​Cj,q​(n)=j⁡(n−1)2​nj.\sum_{q=0}^{j(n-1)}qC_{j,q}(n)=\frac{j(n-1)}{2}n^{j}.

With the coefficients Cj,q​(n)C_{j,q}(n) we define the sum sk,j​(n)s_{k,j}(n) by

sk,j​(n):=∑q=0j⁡(n−1)Cj,q​(n)​xj+q,s_{k,j}(n):=\sum_{q=0}^{j(n-1)}C_{j,q}(n)x_{j+q},

where xr:=r2​k+1x_{r}:=r^{2k+1}. Let us remark that sk,1​(n)=S2​k+1​(n)s_{k,1}(n)=S_{2k+1}(n). Next, we would like to give a suitable expression for the sums sk,2​(n)s_{k,2}(n), which will be used in the following section. It is evident that

C2,q​(n)={q+1,q=0,…,n−2,2​n−q−1,q=n−1,…,2​n−2C_{2,q}(n)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}q+1,\;\;q=0,\ldots,n-2,\\[8.5359pt] 2n-q-1,\;\;q=n-1,\ldots,2n-2\end{array}\right.

and therefore

sk,2​(n)\displaystyle s_{k,2}(n) :⁣=\displaystyle:= ∑q=02​n−2C2,q​(n)​xq+2\displaystyle\sum_{q=0}^{2n-2}C_{2,q}(n)x_{q+2}
=\displaystyle= ∑q=0n−2(q+1)​xq+2+∑q=n−12​n−2(2​n−q−1)​xq+2.\displaystyle\sum_{q=0}^{n-2}(q+1)x_{q+2}+\sum_{q=n-1}^{2n-2}(2n-q-1)x_{q+2}.

Shifting q→q−2q\rightarrow q-2, we get

sk,2​(n)=∑q=1n(q−1)​xq+∑q=n+12​n(2​n−q+1)​xq,s_{k,2}(n)=\sum_{q=1}^{n}(q-1)x_{q}+\sum_{q=n+1}^{2n}(2n-q+1)x_{q},

and since q−1=(2​n−q+1)−(2​n−2​q+2)q-1=(2n-q+1)-(2n-2q+2), we deduce that

sk,2(n)=−∑q=1n(2n−2q+2)xq+∑q=12​n(2n−q+1)xq.s_{k,2}(n)=-\sum_{q=1}^{n}(2n-2q+2)x_{q}+\sum_{q=1}^{2n}(2n-q+1)x_{q}. (2.3)

3. The sums Sk,j​(n)S_{k,j}(n) and S~k,j​(n)\tilde{S}_{k,j}(n)

Let us define a sum

S~k,j​(n):=∑{λ}∈Bj,j​n{λ12​k+1+(λ2−n)2​k+1+⋯+(λj−j​n+n)2​k+1},\tilde{S}_{k,j}(n):=\sum_{\{\lambda\}\in B_{j,jn}}\left\{\lambda_{1}^{2k+1}+(\lambda_{2}-n)^{2k+1}+\cdots+(\lambda_{j}-jn+n)^{2k+1}\right\},

where Bj,j​n:={λk:1≤λ1≤⋯≤λj≤j​n}B_{j,jn}:=\{\lambda_{k}:1\leq\lambda_{1}\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_{j}\leq jn\} and

Sk,j​(n)=∑q=0j−1(j⁡(n+1)q)​sk,j−q​(n).S_{k,j}(n)=\sum_{q=0}^{j-1}{j(n+1)\choose q}s_{k,j-q}(n). (3.1)

It is obvious that

S~k,1​(n)=Sk,1​(n)=sk,1​(n)=S2​k+1​(n).\tilde{S}_{k,1}(n)=S_{k,1}(n)=s_{k,1}(n)=S_{2k+1}(n).
Conjecture 3.1.

For any k≥0k\geq 0 and j≥1j\geq 1, one has

S~k,j​(n)=Sk,j​(n).\tilde{S}_{k,j}(n)=S_{k,j}(n). (3.2)

Let us prove (3.2) in the particular case j=2j=2. Using simple arguments we deduce that

S~k,2​(n)\displaystyle\tilde{S}_{k,2}(n) =\displaystyle= ∑{λ}∈B2,2​n{λ12​k+1+(λ2−n)2​k+1}\displaystyle\sum_{\{\lambda\}\in B_{2,2n}}\left\{\lambda_{1}^{2k+1}+(\lambda_{2}-n)^{2k+1}\right\} (3.3)
=\displaystyle= ∑q=12​n(2​n−q+1)​xq+∑q=12​n(2​n−q+1)​xn−q+1.\displaystyle\sum_{q=1}^{2n}(2n-q+1)x_{q}+\sum_{q=1}^{2n}(2n-q+1)x_{n-q+1}.

Notice that we have several xrx_{r}’s with negative subscript rr in (3.3). Clearly, we must put xr=−x−rx_{r}=-x_{-r}. Taking into account this rule, we rewrite the second sum in (3.3) as

∑q=1n(n+q)​xq−∑q=1n(n−q)​xq=2​∑q=1nq​xq.\sum_{q=1}^{n}(n+q)x_{q}-\sum_{q=1}^{n}(n-q)x_{q}=2\sum_{q=1}^{n}qx_{q}.

Adding to (3.3) the terms

−∑q=1n(2n−2q+2)xq+∑q=1n(2n−2q+2)xq-\sum_{q=1}^{n}(2n-2q+2)x_{q}+\sum_{q=1}^{n}(2n-2q+2)x_{q}

and taking into account (2.3), we finally get

S~k,2​(n)\displaystyle\tilde{S}_{k,2}(n) =\displaystyle= sk,2​(n)+(2​n+2)​∑q=1nxq\displaystyle s_{k,2}(n)+(2n+2)\sum_{q=1}^{n}x_{q}
=\displaystyle= sk,2​(n)+(2​(n+1)1)​sk,1​(n)\displaystyle s_{k,2}(n)+{2(n+1)\choose 1}s_{k,1}(n)
=\displaystyle= Sk,2​(n).\displaystyle S_{k,2}(n).

Therefore, we proved conjecture 3.1 in the particular case j=2j=2.

4. Special case of the sums Sk,j​(n)S_{k,j}(n)

In the case n=1n=1, the sum (3.1) becomes

Sk,j​(1)=∑q=0j−1(2​jq)​(j−q)2​k+1.S_{k,j}(1)=\sum_{q=0}^{j-1}{2j\choose q}(j-q)^{2k+1}. (4.1)

This type of the sums was studied in [2], [14], [15]. To be precise, the authors of these works considered binomial sums of the form

𝒮m​(j)=∑q=02​j(2​jq)​|j−q|m.\mathcal{S}_{m}(j)=\sum_{q=0}^{2j}{2j\choose q}|j-q|^{m}.

It is evident that Sk,j​(1)=𝒮2​k+1​(j)/2S_{k,j}(1)=\mathcal{S}_{2k+1}(j)/2.

Some bibliographical remarks are as follows. Bruckman in [2] asked to prove that 𝒮3​(j)=j2​(2​jj)\mathcal{S}_{3}(j)=j^{2}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}2j\\ j\end{array}\right). Strazdins in [14] solved this problem and conjectured that 𝒮2​k+1​(j)=P~k​(x)|x=j​(2​jj)\mathcal{S}_{2k+1}(j)=\tilde{P}_{k}(x)|_{x=j}{2j\choose j} with some monic polynomial P~k​(x)\tilde{P}_{k}(x) for any k≥0k\geq 0. Tuenter showed in [15] that it is almost true. More exactly, he proved that there exists a sequence of polynomials Pk​(x)P_{k}(x) such that

𝒮2​k+1​(j)=Pk​(x)|x=j​j​(2​jj)=Pk​(x)|x=j​(2​j)!(j−1)!​j!.\mathcal{S}_{2k+1}(j)=P_{k}(x)|_{x=j}j{2j\choose j}=P_{k}(x)|_{x=j}\frac{(2j)!}{(j-1)!j!}.

One can see that polynomial P~k​(x)\tilde{P}_{k}(x) is monic only for k=0,1k=0,1. The following proposition [15] is verified by direct computations.

Proposition 4.1.

The sums Sk,j​(1)S_{k,j}(1) satisfy the recurrence relation

Sk,j​(1)=j2​Sk−1,j​(1)−2​j​(2​j−1)​Sk−1,j−1​(1).S_{k,j}(1)=j^{2}S_{k-1,j}(1)-2j(2j-1)S_{k-1,j-1}(1). (4.2)
Remark 4.2.

This was, in fact, proved for the sums 𝒮2​k+1​(j)\mathcal{S}_{2k+1}(j) in [15].

Let us introduce the sequence of positive integer numbers:

g1=1,gj=j(j−1)!​∏q=1j−1(j+q),j≥2.g_{1}=1,\;\;g_{j}=\frac{j}{(j-1)!}\prod_{q=1}^{j-1}(j+q),\;\;j\geq 2.

As can be checked, this sequence satisfies the recurrence relation

gj+1=2​2​j+1j​gj.g_{j+1}=2\frac{2j+1}{j}g_{j}. (4.3)

Let us write

Sk,j​(1)=Pk,j​gjS_{k,j}(1)=P_{k,j}g_{j}

with some numbers Pk,jP_{k,j} to be calculated. Taking into account (4.3), it can be easily seen that (4.2) is valid if the relation

Pk+1,j=j2​(Pk,j−Pk,j−1)+j​Pk,j−1P_{k+1,j}=j^{2}\left(P_{k,j}-P_{k,j-1}\right)+jP_{k,j-1} (4.4)

holds. Now we need the polynomials studied in [15] which are defined by a recurrence relation

Pk+1​(x)=x2​(Pk​(x)−Pk​(x−1))+x​Pk​(x−1)P_{k+1}(x)=x^{2}\left(P_{k}(x)-P_{k}(x-1)\right)+xP_{k}(x-1) (4.5)

with initial condition P0​(x)=1P_{0}(x)=1. The first eight polynomials yielded by (4.5) are as follows:

P0​(x)=1,P1​(x)=x,P2​(x)=x⁡(2​x−1),P_{0}(x)=1,\;\;P_{1}(x)=x,\;\;P_{2}(x)=x(2x-1),

Remark 4.3.

As was noticed in [15], the polynomials Pk​(x)P_{k}(x) can be obtained as a special case of Dumont-Foata polynomials of three variables [3].

Unfortunately, in the general case we do not know a recursion relation for these polynomials except for the case t=2t=2. One can check that Pk​(t,x)|t=2=Pk​(x)P_{k}(t,x)|_{t=2}=P_{k}(x), where Pk​(x)P_{k}(x) are Tuenter’s polynomials introduced above.

It can be noticed that the coefficients of the polynomials Pk​(t,x)P_{k}(t,x) have a special form. Namely, let

Pk​(t,x)=x⁡(pk,0​(t)​xk−1−pk,1​(t)​xk−2+⋯+(−1)k−1​pk,k−1​(t)).P_{k}(t,x)=x\left(p_{k,0}(t)x^{k-1}-p_{k,1}(t)x^{k-2}+\cdots+(-1)^{k-1}p_{k,k-1}(t)\right). (5.1)

Based on actual calculations, we are led to the following.

Conjecture 5.2.

The coefficients of tt-dependent polynomial (5.1) are given by

pk,j​(t)=rk,j​(t)tj,p_{k,j}(t)=\frac{r_{k,j}(t)}{t^{j}},

where the polynomials rk,j​(t)r_{k,j}(t) are of the form

rk,j​(t)=∑q=0mαk,j,q​t2​q​(t+1)j−3​qr_{k,j}(t)=\sum_{q=0}^{m}\alpha_{k,j,q}t^{2q}(t+1)^{j-3q}

with rational positive nonzero numbers αk,j,q\alpha_{k,j,q}. Here m≥0m\geq 0, by definition, is the result of division of the number jj by 33 with some remainder ll, that is, j=3​m+lj=3m+l.

It should be noticed that the last conjecture is quite strong. With this conjecture the number NkN_{k} of parameters which entirely define the polynomial Pk​(t,x)P_{k}(t,x) for small values of kk is given in the following table:

kk 11 22 33 44 55 66 77 88 9
NkN_{k} 11 2 3 5 7 9 12 15 18

These numbers form the A001840 integer sequence in [13]. We have, in fact, verified conjecture 5.2 up to k=11k=11 and calculated all corresponding coefficients αk,j,q\alpha_{k,j,q}.

It is evident that for all the polynomials Pk​(t,x)P_{k}(t,x) we have pk,0​(t)=k!p_{k,0}(t)=k!. Actual calculations show that

αk,1,0=(k−1)​(k+1)9​k!,k≥2,\alpha_{k,1,0}=\frac{(k-1)(k+1)}{9}k!,\;\;k\geq 2,
αk,2,0=(k−2)​(k+1)​(5​k2+k−3)810​k!,k≥3,\alpha_{k,2,0}=\frac{(k-2)(k+1)(5k^{2}+k-3)}{810}k!,\;\;k\geq 3,

αk,j,0=(k−j)​(k+1)​pj​(k)​k!,k≥j+1\alpha_{k,j,0}=(k-j)(k+1)p_{j}(k)k!,\;\;k\geq j+1

with some polynomial pj​(k)p_{j}(k) of degree 2​j−22j-2.

S4,1​(n)=t220​(2​t3−5​t2+6​t−3),S5,1​(n)=t224​(2​t4−8​t3+17​t2−20​t+10),S_{4,1}(n)=\frac{t^{2}}{20}\left(2t^{3}-5t^{2}+6t-3\right),\;\;S_{5,1}(n)=\frac{t^{2}}{24}\left(2t^{4}-8t^{3}+17t^{2}-20t+10\right),
S6,1​(n)=t2840​(60​t5−350​t4+1148​t3−46584​t2+2764​t−1382),S_{6,1}(n)=\frac{t^{2}}{840}\left(60t^{5}-350t^{4}+1148t^{3}-46584t^{2}+2764t-1382\right),

One usually writes

Sk,1​(n)=12​(k+1)​∑q=0kAq(k+1)​tk−q+1,S_{k,1}(n)=\frac{1}{2(k+1)}\sum_{q=0}^{k}A_{q}^{(k+1)}t^{k-q+1},

where A0(k)=1A^{(k)}_{0}=1 and Ak−1(k)=0A^{(k)}_{k-1}=0. We know quite a lot about the coefficients Aq(k)A_{q}^{(k)}. Jacobi proved that the coefficients Aq(k)A_{q}^{(k)} satisfy the recurrence relation

(2​k+2)​(2​k+1)​Aq(k)=2​(k−q+1)​(2​k−2​q+1)​Aq(k+1)+(k−q+1)​(k−q+2)​Aq−1(k+1)(2k+2)(2k+1)A_{q}^{(k)}=2(k-q+1)(2k-2q+1)A_{q}^{(k+1)}+(k-q+1)(k-q+2)A_{q-1}^{(k+1)}

and tabulated some of them. It was shown by Knuth in [11] that these coefficients satisfy the quite simple implicit recurrence relation

∑q=0r(k−q2​r+1−2​q)​Aq(k)=0,r>0\sum_{q=0}^{r}{k-q\choose 2r+1-2q}A_{q}^{(k)}=0,\;\;r>0 (6.1)

which yields an infinite triangle system of equations from which one easily obtains

A1(k)=−(k−2)​k6,A2(k)=(k−3)​(k−1)​k​(7​k−8)360,A_{1}^{(k)}=-\frac{(k-2)k}{6},\;\;A_{2}^{(k)}=\frac{(k-3)(k-1)k(7k-8)}{360},
A3(k)=−(k−4)​(k−2)​(k−1)​k​(31​k2−89​k+48)15120,A_{3}^{(k)}=-\frac{(k-4)(k-2)(k-1)k(31k^{2}-89k+48)}{15120},
A4(k)=(k−5)​(k−3)​(k−2)​(k−1)​k​(127​k3−691​k2+1038​k−384)604800A_{4}^{(k)}=\frac{(k-5)(k-3)(k-2)(k-1)k(127k^{3}-691k^{2}+1038k-384)}{604800}

etc. Gessel and Viennot showed in [9] that the solution of system (6.1) can be represented as a k×kk\times k determinant

Aq(k)=1(1−k)⋯(q−k)​|(k−q+13)(k−q+11)0⋯0(k−q+25)(k−q+23)(k−q+21)⋯0⋮⋮⋮⋮(k−12​k−1)(k−12​k−3)(k−12​k−5)⋯(k−11)(k2​k+1)(k−12​k−1)(k−12​k−3)⋯(k3)|A_{q}^{(k)}=\frac{1}{(1-k)\cdots(q-k)}\left|\begin{array}[]{ccccc}{k-q+1\choose 3}&{k-q+1\choose 1}&0&\cdots&0\\[2.84544pt] {k-q+2\choose 5}&{k-q+2\choose 3}&{k-q+2\choose 1}&\cdots&0\\[2.84544pt] \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&&\vdots\\[2.84544pt] {k-1\choose 2k-1}&{k-1\choose 2k-3}&{k-1\choose 2k-5}&\cdots&{k-1\choose 1}\\[2.84544pt] {k\choose 2k+1}&{k-1\choose 2k-1}&{k-1\choose 2k-3}&\cdots&{k\choose 3}\end{array}\right|

(see also [5]). A bivariate generating function for the coefficients Aq(k)A_{q}^{(k)} was obtained in [8].

7. The conjectural relationship of the coefficients pk,k−1​(t)p_{k,k-1}(t) to simple symmetric Venn diagrams

Let us rewrite the coefficients pk,k−1​(t)p_{k,k-1}(t) being expressed via nn, that is,

pk,k−1​(n)=pk,k−1​(t)|t=n⁡(n+1).p_{k,k-1}(n)=p_{k,k-1}(t)|_{t=n(n+1)}.

For example,

etc. Looking at these patterns we see that

pk,k−1​(n)=ck​vk​(n)nk−1​(n+1)k−1,p_{k,k-1}(n)=c_{k}\frac{v_{k}(n)}{n^{k-1}(n+1)^{k-1}}, (7.1)

where vk​(n)v_{k}(n) is a monic polynomial of degree 2​k−22k-2. All these polynomials are invariant with respect to the transformation

vk​(n)↦n2​k−2​vk​(1n).v_{k}(n)\mapsto n^{2k-2}v_{k}\left(\frac{1}{n}\right). (7.2)

Also it is worth to remark that the polynomial v4​(n)v_{4}(n) unlike the others, has several fractional coefficients.

Conjecture 7.1.

The polynomials vk​(n)v_{k}(n) are given by

vk​(n)=∑q=12​k−1(2​kq)+(−1)q+12​k+1​n2​k−q−1,v_{k}(n)=\sum_{q=1}^{2k-1}\frac{{2k\choose q}+(-1)^{q+1}}{2k+1}n^{2k-q-1}, (7.3)

while the coefficients ckc_{k} are expressed via the Bernoulli numbers as

ck=(−1)k+1​(2​k+1)​2k​B2​k.c_{k}=(-1)^{k+1}(2k+1)2^{k}B_{2k}. (7.4)

Let us notice that if (7.3) is valid then the invariance of the corresponding polynomial with respect to (7.4) is obvious in virtue of the invariance of binomial coefficients.

Let p=2​k+1p=2k+1. It is known that if pp is prime then

T⁡(p,q)=(p−1q)+(−1)q+1p,p≥5T(p,q)=\frac{{p-1\choose q}+(-1)^{q+1}}{p},\;\;p\geq 5

is the number of qq-points on the left side of a crosscut of the simple symmetric pp-Venn diagram [12]. This integer sequence is known as the A219539 sequence in [13]. It is evident that the row sum

tp:=∑q=1p−2T⁡(p,q)=2p−1−1pt_{p}:=\sum_{q=1}^{p-2}T(p,q)=\frac{2^{p-1}-1}{p}

can be calculated as vk​(n)|n=1v_{k}(n)|_{n=1}. The Fermat quotients (2p−1−1)/p(2^{p-1}-1)/p for prime pp’s form the integer sequence A007663 in [13]. Taking into account (7.1) and (7.4), we get

pk,k−1​(n)|n=1=2​(22​k−1)​B2​k=−G2​k.p_{k,k-1}(n)|_{n=1}=2(2^{2k}-1)B_{2k}=-G_{2k}.

8. Discussion

In the paper we have considered some class of sums Sk,j​(n)S_{k,j}(n) and conjectured a representation of these sums in terms of a sequence of the polynomials {Pk​(t,x):k≥0}\{P_{k}(t,x):k\geq 0\}. This assumption resulted from computational experiments and is supported by a large amount of actual calculations. For n=1n=1, we get the well-known results from [15]. This also confirms our assumptions. The conjectural relationship of several coefficients of the polynomials Pk​(t,x)P_{k}(t,x) being expressed via nn to simple symmetric Venn diagrams is quite unexpected and requires explanation.
